notes:
I've gathered notes on Ezekiel 33, verse by verse. I ran out of searches before I could check several of the sites you listed, so some parts of your brief are thin or missing. The section at the end lists what's not covered.

**Sources and labels.** The "Tradition" labels mostly come from what the sites themselves say. StudyLight tags Adam Clarke as Wesleyan/Methodist and Arminian, and enduringword.com is on your Pentecostal/charismatic list. The rest are my own labels and are worth double-checking: Benson as Methodist, Gill and Spurgeon as Baptist, Smith as Calvary Chapel, Murray as Reformed, Constable as dispensational, Coffman as Churches of Christ. I was only able to fetch David Guzik's Enduring Word page up to verse 29, so I have nothing from him on verses 30–33.

---

## Overview (vv. 1–20)
- Constable says this part repeats ch. 3:16–21 and ch. 18:21–32. He sees it as a hinge: it points back to the judgment messages and forward to the hope messages that follow. This part of Ezekiel's message of warning to the exiles is similar to Ezekiel 3:16-21. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezekiel-33.html
- Utley points out one difference from ch. 18. In this chapter the people admit their sin (cf. v. 10). https://bible.org/seriespage/ezekiel-33

## v. 1
- Pulpit Commentary: after more than two years of messages about foreign nations (chs. 25–32), Ezekiel turns back to his own people. Now his own people are again the object of his care. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezekiel/33-1.html
- Constable: Ezekiel had not spoken to the exiles for about three years (588–585 B.C.), because God had shut his mouth (24:25–27). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezekiel-33.html

## v. 2
- Ellicott: the image is the same as in 3:17. Pulpit adds that Ezekiel returns to that idea and enlarges it. Ezekiel falls back upon the thought of Ezekiel 3:17, but the image is expanded with characteristic fullness. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/33-2.htm
- Clarke (Wesleyan) notes a contrast with ch. 3. Here the PEOPLE choose the watchman; there, the Lord appoints him. When God chooses, the people should approve. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezekiel/33-2.html
- Gill: the watchman stood somewhere high, on the walls or in a tower of a border town, so he could see the enemy coming from far off. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezekiel/33-2.html
- Utley: "the sword" in this chapter echoes ch. 21. It is one of several judgments, along with famine, plague and wild beasts (5:17). https://bible.org/seriespage/ezekiel-33

## v. 3
- Utley: "sword" is a picture for an invading army, here Nebuchadnezzar's. The trumpet is the shofar, or ram's horn, which was used both in worship and in war. https://bible.org/seriespage/ezekiel-33
- Constable: watchmen on city towers watched the horizon and blew the shofar so farm workers could run into the city. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezekiel-33.html

## vv. 4–5
- Guzik: if the watchman warned and people ignored him, their blood was on themselves. This was a great assurance to Ezekiel and Jeremiah because they warned many but few listened. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-33/
- Constable: the phrase "blood on one's head" comes from sacrifice. The person offering laid hands on the animal's head, which showed guilt passing to the substitute. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezekiel-33.html
- Utley: Ezekiel is partly defending his message of judgment. Because he did speak, the people could not blame him or God. Utley adds that "blood" stands for a person's life. https://bible.org/seriespage/ezekiel-33

## v. 6
- Geneva Study Bible: a careless watchman does not let the wicked off. Someone warned who still refuses to obey earns double punishment. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/33-6.htm
- Pulpit (in Ellicott's section): The words imply what we might almost call the agony of self-accusation. The prophet asks himself whether he has acted on the warning which was borne in on his mind at the very beginning of his mission. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/33-6.htm
- Gill: someone taken unwarned has no time to repent and ask for mercy. The watchman must answer for that death. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezekiel/33-6.html
- Coffman: Individual responsibility is the blunt message here. Even if the watchman does not warn, that cannot excuse the victim. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezekiel/33-2.html

## v. 7
- The Preacher's Homiletical Commentary says the "I" is emphatic. Ezekiel's spiritual appointment is weightier because it comes from God, not from the people. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/ezekiel-33.html
- Guzik: the watchman did not get his knowledge by studying Babylon's armies. He heard from God that judgment was near and had to announce it. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-33/
- **What "watchman" means today.** Guzik warns against people who call themselves watchmen today but mainly hunt for error in others. He thinks the biblical role is mainly proclaiming God's truth. He also says unfair reports make a watchman unbelievable when real danger comes. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-33/
- **Applied to every believer.** Chuck Smith (Calvary Chapel) applies it to Christian witnessing in general. God has not commissioned us, really, to argue people in to the kingdom of heaven, or to pressure or to force people into the kingdom of heaven. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezekiel/33-2.html

## vv. 8–9
- Utley: "you will surely die" uses a Hebrew construction for emphasis (a repeated verb). https://bible.org/seriespage/ezekiel-33
- Constable links this to Paul in Acts 20:26. He notes that chs. 4–24 contain the warnings Ezekiel faithfully gave. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezekiel-33.html
- **Applied to pastors.**
  - Calvin, on 1 Tim 4:16, cites Ezek 33:8. A pastor "saves himself" by doing his duty faithfully, so he escapes the vengeance threatened in Ezekiel. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/kjv/1-timothy/4-16.html
  - The Biblical Illustrator quotes Latimer telling clergy to learn watchfulness even from the devil, who never rests going round his "diocese." https://biblehub.com/sermons/ezekiel/33-8.htm

## v. 10
- Constable: This is the first indication in the book that they were conscious of their own sins. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezekiel-33.html
- Utley: in ch. 18 the people blamed their ancestors, but here they admit their own sin. "Rotting away" comes from the curses in Lev 26:39–42. https://bible.org/seriespage/ezekiel-33
- **Two readings of the people's cry:**
  - Guzik: an accusing question, as if God made judgment so harsh that repentance was impossible. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-33/
  - Bridgeway: real sorrow that is sliding toward despair. For the first time, the exiles show sorrow for their past sin. Some are even tempted to despair. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezekiel/33-2.html
- Constable quotes Wiersbe on the difference between regret, remorse and true repentance. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezekiel-33.html

## v. 11
- Gill: God's oath shows the "certainty, reality, and sincerity" of the statement. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/33-11.htm
- Guzik: this is said first about judgment on Judah in this life, but it also applies to eternal judgment. God not delighting in death does not mean death won't happen. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-33/
- **Where traditions differ: does God sincerely want every sinner saved?**
  - Reformed: John Murray argues for a universal will. It is absolutely and universally true that God does not delight in or desire the death of a wicked person. He says the call to repent expresses a will that all should repent. https://www.monergism.com/ezekiel-1823-32-and-3311
  - Baptist (Spurgeon): It is one or the other: turn or burn. God, with all his love to men, cannot discover any third course. He argues God would not plead with people unless he really wanted them to escape. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezekiel/33-11.html
  - Matthew Henry: God is "sincere and in earnest" in calling sinners to repent. If they perish, it is their own doing. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezekiel/33-11.html
  - A sermon by Dibdin in the Biblical Illustrator applies it in broadly universal terms: tell the worst sinner that Christ redeemed him and all mankind. https://biblehub.com/sermons/ezekiel/33-11.htm
  - Utley links it to verses about God wanting all to be saved (1 Tim 2:4; 2 Pet 3:9). He notes the Hebrew word for "turn" means a change of action. https://bible.org/seriespage/ezekiel-33
  - Desiring God uses the verse to urge Christians to share the gospel. https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/we-murder-with-words-unsaid

## v. 12
- Guzik: this answers fatalism, the idea that the good stay good, the bad stay bad and nothing can change it. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-33/
- Keil & Delitzsch: vv. 12–20 are there so people don't twist the comfort of v. 11 into false confidence in their own righteousness. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/33-13.htm
- Utley: this verse is not about building up guilt or merit. It is about lifestyle relational faith. https://bible.org/seriespage/ezekiel-33

## v. 13 (the key point of disagreement, with v. 18)
- **Can a truly righteous person fall away? Readings differ:**
  - Methodist (Benson): trusting your own righteousness or spiritual progress is one step toward a fall, and generally issues in apostacy. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/33-13.htm
  - Wesleyan (Clarke): the warning is about someone who keeps religious rules and treats others fairly but still sins in other ways. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezekiel/33-13.html
  - Matthew Henry: the promise holds if he be really as good as he seems to be. He gives the Pharisees as an example of trusting in one's own righteousness. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezekiel/33-13.html
  - Gill: that righteousness cannot justify a person or protect him from wrath. It will be as though it never existed. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezekiel/33-13.html
  - Dispensational (Constable): the issue here is not earning eternal salvation or losing it by the way one lives. It is rather the consequences of individual behavior in this life, which the Mosaic Law promised. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezekiel-33.html
  - Guzik: neither "he shall surely live" nor "you shall surely die" was final or unchangeable. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-33/
  - Trapp reads "trusts in his righteousness" as thinking it bought him permission to sin. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/trapp_john/eze-33.cfm
  - Utley: faith must go on daily, from first repentance to ongoing repentance. https://bible.org/seriespage/ezekiel-33

## vv. 14–16
- Utley:
  - Here there is no line between "secular" and "sacred" duty.
  - A "pledge" was security taken for a loan, such as a millstone, a garment, land, an animal or even children. Taking it could put a family's life at risk.
  - Stolen goods had to be returned with a penalty.

  https://bible.org/seriespage/ezekiel-33
- Matthew Henry: returning the pledge is evidence of real repentance. Walking "without committing iniquity" means not being ruled by any sin, though not being free of weakness. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezekiel/33-13.html
- Constable: the person who repents would not die early and would receive life as a reward. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezekiel-33.html

## vv. 17–19
- Guzik: God was fair. The people were the unfair ones, because they let fate or the past decide a person's destiny. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-33/
- Coffman: the stress is on what a person is now, not what he was before. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/ezekiel/33-13.html

## v. 20
- Guzik: this standard was fair under the old covenant, which rested heavily on works. It is also fair under the new covenant, where works show faith is real (James 2). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-33/
- Constable: God does not blame one person for another's sins. He applies this to people today who blame others for how they live. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezekiel-33.html

## v. 21
- Constable:
  - He dates the news to about January 19, 585 B.C., about five months after the city fell.
  - Some count the gap as 18 months. He thinks five is more likely.

  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezekiel-33.html
- Guzik calls this a sad and tragic vindication of the prophet. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-33/

## v. 22
- Constable: this fulfils 24:25–27 and ends the silence of 3:26–27. Quoting Wiersbe, he says Ezekiel could now have a "pastoral" ministry after about seven and a half years. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezekiel-33.html

## vv. 23–24
- Guzik: the survivors in Judah thought they would rebuild Israel. God had promised the restoration would come through the returning exiles instead. Jeremiah 40–44 describes these people. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-33/
- Constable links it to Matt 3:9 and John 8:33, 39, other places where people claimed Abraham as their father. He quotes Block on their smugness compared with Abraham's total dependence on God. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezekiel-33.html

## vv. 25–26
- Constable: the people broke the Law (the commandments, plus Lev 17 on eating blood). Holding the land depended on obedience (Deut 27–29). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezekiel-33.html
- Guzik: the question is asked twice to stress that they would *not* possess the land. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-33/

## vv. 27–29
- Guzik: the survivors' judgment was only put off, and Jeremiah 40–44 shows it came. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-33/
- Constable ties the sword, wild beasts and disease to the covenant curses in Leviticus 26. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezekiel-33.html

## vv. 30–31
- Constable: the exiles talked about Ezekiel in private and in public, but their hearts stayed set on their own desires and gain. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezekiel-33.html

## v. 32
- Constable: Entertainers expect no response to their performances beyond applause, but preachers expect people to change. He links it to James 1:22–25 and calls it one of the Bible's sharpest charges against God's people. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezekiel-33.html
- Chuck Smith: right now they're just listening, and the prophet is entertainment to them. https://studylight.org/commentaries/csc/ezekiel-33.html

## v. 33
- Coffman: even the exiles didn't believe the prophecy about the remnant in Judah being wiped out. "Behold it cometh" means it would surely happen, like everything else Ezekiel foretold. https://studylight.org/commentaries/bcc/ezekiel-33.html

---

## Other views: Church Fathers (newadvent.org; these are shared by Catholic and Orthodox readers)
- **vv. 6–8, Gregory the Great:** he quotes the watchman passage as his reason for rebuking a sinner by letter. For when the pastor refuses to rebuke those that sin, there is no doubt that in holding his peace he slays them. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/360201034.htm
- **v. 6, John Chrysostom (On the Priesthood):** a priest cannot plead ignorance, because he is placed there to sound the trumpet. And therefore his chastisement is inevitable, though he that perishes happen to be but one. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/19226.htm
- **v. 6, Augustine (City of God I.9):** For watchmen or overseers of the people are appointed in churches, that they may unsparingly rebuke sin. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/120101.htm
- **vv. 8–9, Augustine (Sermon 87):** he treats the watchman passage as a charge to himself to speak. If he warns and the hearer does not change, Augustine has delivered his own soul. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/160387.htm

## Not covered
- **Lutheran:** nothing found.
- **Pentecostal:** nothing beyond Guzik and Smith, whose sources (enduringword.com, the Calvary Chapel network) don't call themselves Pentecostal.
- **Anglican:** only the Latimer quote at vv. 8–9.
- **Modern scholarship:** nothing from bibleodyssey.org or netbible.org notes.
- **Catholic and Orthodox:** nothing from catholic.com or oca.org, so only the Church Fathers above.
- **Popular teaching:** nothing on prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace readings.
- **Precept Austin:** not consulted.
